newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: FEATURE - Puerto Rico faces life minus big tax break.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Puerto Rico faces life minus big tax break.

text.p: When Congress slammed Puerto Rico's special manufacturing tax break as "corporate welfare" and voted to phase it out last summer, many people expected the island's economy to flounder.

Boosted by the tax break, known as Section 936 of the IRS code, the United States territory had blossomed as a home to factories built by more than 500 U.S. companies, transforming itself from "the poorhouse of the Caribbean" in the 1940s to the area with the highest per capita income in Latin America.

In particular, the island's proximity to the United States and relatively educated workforce combined with the lure of the tax break to make it one of the world's major pharmaceutical manufacturing centres, home to facilities of giants such as Eli Lilly and Co and SmithKline Beecham.
MINIMUM WAGE BILL PHASES OUT CORPORATE TAX BREAK

But the new U.S. minimum wage bill signed into law last August included a 10-year phaseout of the tax provision, which exempted U.S. corporations from federal taxes on earnings from Puerto Rican operations and interest earned on qualified investments on the island.

With unemployment much higher than on the U.S. mainland -- unemployment in December was 10.1 percent -- 42 percent of the population receiving public assistance and government jobs accounting for 19 percent of employment, it was not much of a stretch to imagine the repeal of 936 would be catastrophic.
Manufacturing accounts for about 42 percent of Puerto Rico's GDP, and 16 percent of its employment. Local economists estimate that 936 companies accounted for about 110,000 of Puerto Rico's jobs.

"Before there was an economic model that emphasised only one sector and that one sector was assisted by, effectively, one economic incentive tool," said Carlos Vivoni, Secretary of the Department of Economic Development and Commerce, told Reuters, describing government plans to increase the contributions of sectors such as tourism.
ECONOMY SHOWS SIGNS OF SURVIVING TAX BREAK'S END

But six months after the announcement, the worst has not happened. Some U.S. firms, having lost the tax break on interest, have withdrawn millions from the commonwealth's financial system, prompting the island's government to propose measures to foster a local corporate debt market.
But overall, officials and analysts said, the commonwealth's economy has continued to show improvement and business had not flagged.

Jaime Morgan-Stubbe, administrator and chief executive officer of the Puerto Rican government's Economic Development Administration Industrial Development Co., said employment in pharmaceuticals and electronics companies in Puerto Rico had risen rather than fallen since Congress had approved a five-year phasedown of part of 936 in 1993, with no sign of a decline since August.
"We have seen stability in the last few years," he said.
Morgan-Stubbe also noted that corporations have continued to make capital investments in Puerto Rico in spite of the prospect of a 936 rollback.
"We've had over the last three years, well over $1.5 billion in capital investment by the manufacturing sector in Puerto Rico," he said.
ANALYSTS REASSURED BY STABILITY SINCE 936 REPEAL
Roy Chun, an analyst who follows Puerto Rico's municipal bonds at Standard & Poor's, said the phaseout of 936 remained a concern, but agreed the worst has not happened.

"No company has come out and said outright that we're leaving," he said. Standard & Poor's had put the island's credit on a negative outlook in 1995 out of concern over a 936 rollback, but changed its outlook as it became clearer the impact would not be as dire as feared.

"After they passed the bill, as a 10-year phaseout, we felt that the way the island economy has been performing and the long phaseout period really gives them time and the ability to potentially address the issues," he said.
"Things are fairly positive," Chun said, noting that unemployment, though still high by standards on the U.S. mainland, is at a near-record low and other economic indicators have been strong.

"Over the last five years, they've increased general fund revenues by 37 percent, almost, and included in that is a pretty substantial tax cut in 1996. That really shows the economy has been doing well," Chun said.
10-YEAR PHASEOUT SEEN GIVING TIME FOR ECONOMIC OVERHAUL
Similarly, in a report issued last month, A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc fixed-income researcher Brad Bode said his rating outlook for Puerto Rico bonds remained stable.

"We continue to believe the commonwealth has ample time to find other sources of economic growth," the report said. Noting the cost of relocating facilities and higher U.S. wage scales, it said, "We have not seen, nor do we expect to see, a mass exodus of companies due to the eventual elimination of the tax benefits."

But analysts also noted Puerto Rico's debt ratings remain low compared with those of most U.S. states, due to financial concerns including major infrastructure needs, a $5 billion unfunded pension liability and plans to privatise its public health care system.
ALTERNATIVE TAX BREAKS AVAILABLE FOR CORPORATIONS

Puerto Rican officials also noted the phaseout of 936 did not leave U.S. companies without tax options for their businesses in Puerto Rico. By changing the status of their operations on the island to Puerto Rican corporations, companies including SmithKline and Hewlett-Packard Co were able to take advantage of two other sections of the tax code -- 954 and 901 -- which benefit foreign subsidiaries of U.S.-based firms.
The subsidiaries then become subject to local taxes, but Puerto Rico's 1987 Tax Incentive Act provides a 90 percent local exemption on profits of firms that manufacture on the island.
